newsitem.title: USA: Jewish leader sees end to Swiss bank secrecy.
newsitem.headline: Jewish leader sees end to Swiss bank secrecy.

text.p: The Jewish leader who led the fight to open Swiss bank records on the assets of Holocaust victims predicted on Thursday that the end of Swiss bank secrecy was near.

In an interview with Reuters, World Jewish Congress President Edgar Bronfman Sr. also called on the Vatican finally to open up its closely-guarded Second World War archives and said he wanted to discuss the issue with Pope John Paul and Vatican officials.

Bronfman, the billionaire chairman of the Seagram Co., said he was gratified the Swiss had finally -- 52 years after the war -- started to publish the names of holders of dormant Holocaust-era accounts. He predicted the world-wide publication of 1,872 names was just a start.

"We are going to see Swiss bank secrecy come tumbling down when they publish the names of 20,000 dormant Swiss accounts in October. The effect is going to be electrifying," he said by telephone from his U.S. summer home.
He added that he did not think that the names of foreign account holders published on Wednesday in 40 newspapers around the world and on the Internet was a final tally.
"The auditors are going to find many more accounts. The process has just begun. None of the banks are saying, 'Here is everything we have' and we would not believe them if they did," he said.

Bronfman began his campaign in 1995 after the Swiss Bankers' Association rebuffed his pleas to open their books and account for the money deposited by Jews in their banks after Hitler took power in Germany.

"It makes me laugh that they (the Swiss Bankers' Association) tried to buy us off with $32 million they said they found in 774 accounts," he said of an offer he rejected at a frosty September 1995 meeting in which he was not even offered a chair.
"They are now facing returning $60 million plus hundreds of millions of dollars in interest from 1,872 accounts with more to come," he added.

Bronfman said, "Had they (the Swiss bankers) acted honestly in the beginning it would have cost them less. They didn't figure that the United States is the United States and that we had powerful people on our side, including President Clinton and New York Sen. Alfonse D'Amato."

Clinton and D'Amato, the chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, joined the battle, with Clinton opening the U.S. National Archives to researchers who discovered extensive Swiss dealings with Nazi Germany during the war, especially in the laundering of looted gold.
Bronfman said Swiss credibility had been greatly damaged because the bankers never gave an accurate figure of the acounts they held.

He added he wanted the Vatican to open its war files, saying, "I have been curious about how many Nazis went to South America with Vatican passports as has been charged. Recently released documents raise questions that must be examined."

Bronfman was referring to a recently released U.S. Treasury Department document that claimed the Vatican held gold and money for safekeeping for Croatian fascists after the war. The Vatican denied the report.
"We owe it to history and memory to pursue the opening of the Vatican files," he added.
